controversies/barth-brunner-natural-theo: Can human beings know anything true of God apart from his revelation in Jesus Christ, and is there a “point of contact” for the gospel in fallen humanity?
Barth vs Brunner: Is there a natural theology?

In 1934, in the middle of the German church struggle, Emil Brunner argued for a limited revelation in creation and a point of contact; Karl Barth answered with a thunderous “No!”. The exchange crystallised a debate that runs from Romans 1 through Aquinas, Calvin and Vatican I.
Brunner: a point of contact

God’s creation truly reveals him, and sinners remain addressable, responsible persons — the formal image of God. Calvin taught a revelation in creation and a sense of deity. Without some point of contact the gospel could not even be heard, and responsibility for sin would be unintelligible. Grace restores nature; it does not abolish it.
Calvin, Institutes 1.3-5

Barth: No!

God is known only where God makes himself known — in Jesus Christ, the one Word of God. Every “point of contact” and every natural theology ends by domesticating God to human projects; in 1934 that meant the German Christians’ God of race and nation. The church must listen to no other voice.

controversies/apologetic-method-debate/q: Should Christian apologetics begin with neutral reason and evidence, with the presupposition of Scripture, or with neither?
controversies/apologetic-method-debate/t: How should Christians defend the faith?
controversies/apologetic-method-debate/s: Modern Protestant apologetics divides into classical, evidential, cumulative-case, presuppositional and Reformed-epistemology approaches, with fideist critics of the whole enterprise; the debate restates old tensions between Justin and Tertullian, Aquinas and Pascal.

Peter told us to give a reason for the hope that is in us, and Paul reasoned in the synagogue and the Areopagus. God made us rational; arguments from the cosmos and the historical evidence for the resurrection meet unbelievers on common ground and remove barriers to faith.
Long tradition from Aquinas to Butler

There is no neutral ground. The unbeliever knows God but suppresses the truth, and his reasoning borrows capital from the Christian worldview. Rather than submitting God to the court of autonomous reason, the apologist should show that only the God of Scripture makes reason itself possible.

Most believers have never followed an argument for God, yet they are not irrational: belief in God can be properly basic. Kierkegaard warned that turning faith into the conclusion of probabilities betrays its passion. Arguments may help defend, but faith rests on God’s own witness.
controversies/apologetic-method-debate/t: Tertullian: “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?”
Van Til’s The Defense of the Faith.

controversies/apologetic-method-debate/r: Unresolved and increasingly eclectic: many apologists combine methods, and the five-views framework is itself contested. Catholic teaching rejects strong fideism (Vatican I) while affirming that faith exceeds reason.
controversies/apologetic-method-debate/c: Shaped evangelical seminaries, debate culture and campus ministries.
Influenced how churches engage secularism, Islam and other religions.
controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/ques: Can human beings obey God by the nature he gave them, or does salvation require a grace that heals and moves the will?
controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/summ: The decisive Western debate on grace and free will (c.411-431), in which the North African church and Rome rejected Pelagius and Caelestius, and Augustine’s teaching on original sin and grace became normative in the Latin West.
controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/side: Pelagius and Caelestius

We honour God’s grace by honouring what he made: a nature able to choose the good. God is just and does not command the impossible. To say we cannot obey is to slander our Creator and to excuse sin. Christ forgives our past and shows us the way; we must now walk in it.
"Ought" implies "can": a just God would not command what is impossible.
Inherited guilt would make God unjust to infants.
Augustine’s "give what you command" breeds passivity.
Universal sin and death suggest a corrupted inheritance (Rom 5).
The Church baptises infants for remission of sins.
Paul’s testimony of a divided will (Rom 7).

Augustine and the African bishops

We do not deny free will; we deny that a wounded will can heal itself. If righteousness came through nature, Christ died in vain. Grace is not merely a lesson set before the eyes but love poured into the heart by the Spirit. We pray for the conversion of others because God, not they, gives it.
Salvation by grace would be emptied if nature sufficed (Gal 2:21).
Infant baptism presupposes inherited sin.
The Church’s prayers ask God for faith and perseverance.

controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/time: Augustine’s Confessions includes the prayer "give what you command", which offends Pelagius in Rome.

controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/reso: Pelagianism was condemned by African councils, Rome and Ephesus (431). Augustine’s doctrine of the necessity of grace became normative in the West; his strong predestinarianism was received only in moderated form at Orange (529). The Eastern churches condemned Pelagianism but never adopted Augustine’s account of inherited guilt.
controversies/augustine-vs-pelagius/cons: Original sin and the necessity of grace became fixed in Latin theology.
"Pelagian" became the Western theological insult par excellence, used in every later controversy.

controversies/calvinism-vs-arminianism-d: Does God elect unconditionally and save by irresistible grace, or does he elect those he foresees will believe, with grace that can be resisted?
Calvinism vs Arminianism at Dort

A Dutch Reformed dispute between the followers of Arminius (Remonstrants) and Gomarus (Counter-Remonstrants), entangled with Dutch politics, decided at the international Synod of Dort (1618-19), whose canons became the classic statement of Calvinism.
Remonstrants (Arminians)

We confess salvation by grace alone. But Scripture says God loves the world, wills all to be saved, and that Christ died for all. Grace goes before every good thought, yet it can be refused, as Israel resisted the Spirit. Election is in Christ: God chose to save believers. Otherwise God’s invitations are insincere and he becomes the author of sin.
Universal texts (John 3:16; 1 Tim 2:4; 1 John 2:2).
Warnings against apostasy (Heb 6).
Moral character of God.
Election then rests on human decision.
Grace that may fail cannot guarantee salvation.
John 3:16
1 Timothy 2:4
Acts 7:51
Hebrews 6:4-6
Counter-Remonstrants (Synod of Dort)

Faith itself is God’s gift. If God elected on the basis of foreseen faith, the difference between saved and lost would lie in the human will, not in grace. Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but God intended it to save his elect infallibly; the Spirit regenerates them effectually and keeps them to the end. This alone gives God the glory and his people a firm comfort.
Election "not because of works" (Rom 9:11).
Faith is a gift (Eph 2:8; Phil 1:29).

Canons of Dort adopted; Remonstrant ministers deposed; Johan van Oldenbarnevelt executed; Grotius imprisoned.
Remonstrants tolerated again; Remonstrant Brotherhood established.

Dort decided for the Counter-Remonstrants within the Dutch Reformed Church, and its canons became one of the Three Forms of Unity. But Arminianism survived in the Remonstrant Brotherhood, among Anglicans and, through John Wesley, became the majority soteriology of Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal Christianity. The debate remains open across evangelicalism.
Defined "Calvinism" as a set of five doctrines.
Political crisis in the Dutch Republic.
A lasting fault line in English Protestantism (Laudians, Puritans), Methodism (Wesley vs Whitefield) and modern evangelicalism.
controversies/justification-wittenberg-v: Is a sinner justified by faith alone through the imputed righteousness of Christ, or by grace that renews the person inwardly, received in faith and working through love?

The central doctrinal conflict of the Reformation, from Luther’s 1517-20 writings through the Augsburg Confession (1530), the failed Regensburg colloquy (1541) and Trent’s Decree on Justification (1547), to the Joint Declaration of 1999.

A troubled conscience cannot rest on its own renewal, which is always incomplete. God justifies the ungodly: he forgives and counts us righteous for Christ’s sake, received by faith alone. This faith unites us to Christ and is never idle; it serves the neighbour freely. To make inner renewal the ground of acceptance is to put our trust in ourselves.

Grace is wholly gratuitous: no one merits the first grace. But God does not merely declare; he makes righteous, pouring charity into our hearts by the Spirit. Faith is the root, yet faith without love is dead. Those justified grow, can fall, and are restored; they merit eternal life only because God crowns his own gifts.
The unity of forgiveness and renewal.
Regensburg Colloquy: Contarini and Melanchthon agree on "double justification", rejected by Rome and Luther.
Trent, Session VI: Decree on Justification.
Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification signed in Augsburg.

Trent fixed the division in 1547. After four centuries, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church declared in 1999 a "consensus in basic truths" and that the mutual condemnations do not apply to each other’s teaching as presented, while differences of emphasis (simul iustus et peccator, merit, assurance) remain. Many confessional Lutherans and evangelicals regard the agreement as inadequate.
The confessional division of the West.
Distinct pieties: Protestant assurance and preaching; Catholic sacramental growth and penance.
A model for later ecumenical method ("differentiated consensus").
